scope_note: Media distance limits are given in the exhibit as a reference table, so items test selecting against constraints rather than reciting distances.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which medium is the least costly one that will carry this link over the measured distance?

exhibit.content:
A 1 Gbps link is needed between two buildings on one campus. The
cable route measured along the duct is 340 m.

    Media                       Practical maximum run
    ------------------------    ---------------------
    Copper twisted pair         100 m
    Multimode fibre             550 m
    Single-mode fibre           10 km and beyond

options.text: Copper twisted pair, since 1 Gbps is well within its rated speed for this link.
Multimode fibre, which spans the distance without single-mode optics.
Single-mode fibre, the only medium rated beyond 100 m.
Copper twisted pair with a repeater placed at the midpoint of the run.

items.explanation: The run is 340 m, which is beyond copper's 100 m limit but comfortably inside multimode's 550 m, and multimode optics cost less than single-mode, so it is the cheapest medium that actually reaches. Option A ignores distance entirely and considers only speed, which copper does support but cannot deliver over 340 m. Option C would work but pays for reach the campus does not need. Option D adds active equipment mid-duct, which introduces a powered device and a failure point where a passive fibre run needs neither.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What best explains why neither port will come up?

exhibit.content:
A contractor ran copper twisted pair between the ground-floor comms
room and a cabinet on the third floor of an adjacent wing. The measured
run is 145 m. Both switch ports are configured identically and neither
comes up; swapping the transceivers and the patch leads changes nothing.

    Media                       Practical maximum run
    ------------------------    ---------------------
    Copper twisted pair         100 m
    Multimode fibre             550 m
    Single-mode fibre           10 km and beyond

options.text: The two switch ports have been left in mismatched VLANs.
The copper run needs a crossover cable rather than a straight-through one.
Autonegotiation is disabled, so the ports never agree on a speed.
The run is 45 m beyond the copper limit, so no reliable link forms.

items.explanation: Twisted pair is specified to 100 m, and this run is 145 m, so signal attenuation prevents a link establishing at all no matter what is fitted at the ends, which is exactly why swapping transceivers and leads changed nothing. Option A describes a VLAN mismatch, which leaves ports up while blocking traffic rather than keeping them down. Option B invokes cable pinout, which modern switches resolve automatically and which would not survive the swap testing already done. Option C describes a mismatch that the exhibit rules out by stating both ports are configured identically.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. How do the two segments compare in the number of collision domains they create?

exhibit.content:
Segment A                          Segment B

      +-------+                          +--------+
      |  HUB  |                          | SWITCH |
      +---+---+                          +---+----+
     /   / \   \                        /   / \   \
   PC1 PC2 PC3 PC4                    PC5 PC6 PC7 PC8

Each device is attached by its own cable, and every port on both
devices is running at 100 Mbps.

options.text: Segment A has four and segment B has one, because the switch merges its ports.
Both have four, because each device is attached by its own dedicated cable.
Segment A has one and segment B has four, because each switch port is its own.
Both have one, because both devices join all their ports into a single domain.

items.explanation: A hub repeats every received signal out of all other ports, so all four stations on segment A share one collision domain regardless of having separate cables. A switch forwards selectively and each port forms its own point-to-point link, giving segment B four separate domains. Option A reverses the two devices. Option B assumes a dedicated cable is enough, but the hub's shared repeating is what defines the domain. Option D describes two hubs and ignores the switch entirely.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which port is fitted with a fibre transceiver rather than a copper connection?

exhibit.content:
SW9# show interfaces status
Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi0/21    reception          connected    10         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/22    meeting room       connected    10         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/23    print room         connected    20         a-full  a-100 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/25    link to annexe     connected    1            full   1000 1000BaseSX

items.explanation: The Type column records the physical media, and Gi0/25 reads 1000BaseSX, an optical standard, while every other port reads 10/100/1000BaseTX, where TX denotes twisted pair. The port's description, link to annexe, fits a run between buildings. Options B and D are both copper access ports negotiating at gigabit, and option C is a copper port that settled at 100 Mbps, which reflects the device plugged into it rather than the media fitted.
